title: Dhoba: washing, payment and ceremonial work
description: Dhoba community history in Odisha through village payments, caste exclusion, ceremonial water, Gandi worship and changing laundry work.
author: Ahimanikya Satapathy
lead: Washing clothes could involve more than a payment for clean garments. Accounts from Odisha describe work tied to the harvest, family ceremonies and worship at the washing place. They also reveal unequal relationships within village life.

paragraphs.text: A study of Daanla in Keonjhar, investigated in 1962 and published in 1968, records one Dhoba household. Its account of the village washerman specifies six seers of paddy from each household after harvest, alongside occasional payments in cash and kind. Washing at a birth or funeral brought two seers of rice and 25 paise.

The same study says Pano and Kolha families were excluded from the service. That exclusion is part of the history of the arrangement, alongside its payments and ceremonial importance. This single village account cannot establish either the rates or the relationships across Odisha.

The Bhadrak District Gazetteer describes a distinction between cleaning a garment and fulfilling a ritual requirement. It reports that some households washed their clothes themselves but still called on a Dhoba to sprinkle water after occasions such as birth or death. The passage concerns ritual beliefs about contamination, not physical dirt or an inherent quality of a person.

This helps explain why an account of the community cannot stop at a list of washing techniques. The service could have a recognised place in a ceremony even when the practical cleaning had been done by someone else.

sections.title: The washing stone and Gandi Puja

paragraphs.text: In Ganjam, the district gazetteer describes Pusha Purnima worship of Nitei Dhobani beside a river, canal or pond used for washing. It calls the washing stone a gandi and gives Gandi Puja as another name for the observance. The working place and its implement are therefore part of this regional account of devotion; it does not establish a founding story for the community.

The Ganjam account describes collecting clothes from homes and returning them washed, sometimes ironed. It contrasts payments in kind in rural areas with cash in towns, and records some workers opening urban laundries instead of making household rounds. Agriculture also supported livelihoods. The passage supplies no dates for these changes, so it should not be read as a current employment survey.
These accounts describe work and ritual, not a single founding event. Local histories are needed to trace settlement and change. Neither a surname nor laundry work identifies someone’s caste.
